title: Good News and Humanity's Rejection of God
summary_text: Paul writes as an apostle with God's gospel about Jesus Christ, David's descendant, declared the Son of God through His resurrection. He hopes to visit Rome and says the gospel brings salvation and reveals God's righteousness through faith. Paul then turns to God's wrath against people who know Him through what He made but trade His glory for idols. God gives them over to shameful desires, including same-sex acts among women and men. He also gives them over to corrupt minds, and they do and praise evil though they know it deserves death.
key_points: Paul's gospel concerns Jesus, descended from David and declared the Son of God in power through the Spirit of holiness by His resurrection.
Paul wants to visit Rome to share encouragement through faith and preach the gospel among Gentiles.
God's gospel brings salvation to believers and reveals His righteousness through faith.
People reject the Creator's visible evidence and worship created things, bringing God's wrath against their wickedness.
God gives people over to dishonorable sexual desires and corrupt thinking, with widespread wrongdoing and approval of evil.

title: God Judges Deeds Rather Than Outward Status
summary_text: People who judge others for sins they also do condemn themselves, Paul says. God leads them toward repentance and judges their deeds fairly, giving eternal life or wrath. Doing the law, rather than just hearing it, leads to being declared righteous; Gentiles without it also have a conscience that accuses or defends them. Paul asks Jewish teachers why they break the laws they teach and so dishonor God. He says circumcision counts with obedience and must concern the heart through the Spirit.
key_points: People who judge others while doing the same wrongs cannot escape God's judgment.
God shows no favoritism and judges each person's deeds, bringing eternal life or wrath for wickedness.
Doing the law, rather than merely hearing it, leads to being declared righteous, and Gentile consciences also bear witness.
Paul challenges teachers who claim the law's wisdom but dishonor God by breaking it.
Lawbreaking turns circumcision into uncircumcision; obedience counts even for the uncircumcised, and true circumcision concerns the heart through the Spirit.

title: All Sin, but God Justifies Through Faith
summary_text: The Jews received God's words, and their lack of faith cannot undo His faithfulness. Paul rejects the claim that God is unfair to judge sin, or that good results can excuse evil. Scripture shows that Jews and Greeks are all under sin, and the law shows guilt rather than justifying people before God. Through redemption in Jesus Christ, God reveals His righteousness and freely justifies believers by grace, putting them in right standing with Him through faith. No one can boast, since Jews and Gentiles share one God and one way of faith that upholds His law.
key_points: God remains faithful despite human failure, and Paul rejects using God's righteousness as an excuse for evil.
Scripture shows Jews and Greeks alike under sin, falling short of God's glory, with no one able to claim innocence.
The law holds people accountable and reveals sin, but works of the law do not justify them before God.
God presents Jesus as an atoning sacrifice through His blood, showing His righteousness as He justifies those who have faith in Jesus.
God justifies the circumcised and uncircumcised through faith, excluding boasting and upholding the law.

title: Abraham's Faith Is Credited as Righteousness
summary_text: God credited Abraham's faith as righteousness apart from works, and David called those with forgiven sins blessed. This came before circumcision, so Abraham is the father of those who share his faith, circumcised or not. God's promise rests on faith and grace, rather than law. Abraham still trusted God's promise, though he was old and Sarah could not bear a child. Paul says God also credits righteousness to those who trust Him as the One who raised Jesus, who died for their trespasses and rose for their justification.
key_points: Abraham's faith and David's words about forgiven sins show the blessing of God crediting righteousness apart from works.
Abraham received circumcision as a seal of righteousness already credited through faith while he was uncircumcised.
The promise rests on faith and grace, while law brings wrath and transgression requires law.
Abraham trusts God's promise despite his old age and Sarah's inability to bear children.
God also credits righteousness to those who believe He raised Jesus, who died for their trespasses and rose for their justification.

title: Peace Through Jesus and Grace Beyond Sin
summary_text: Being justified through faith brings peace with God, access to His grace, and hope of His glory. Paul says suffering builds endurance, character, and hope, while God gives His love through the Holy Spirit. Christ died for sinners, proving God's love; those reconciled to God through His death will be saved through His life. Paul contrasts Adam's sin, which brought death, with Jesus's obedience, which brings righteousness and life. The law increases trespass, but grace grows greater still and leads to eternal life through Jesus.
key_points: Faith brings peace with God, and suffering leads through endurance and character to hope.
Christ dies for ungodly sinners, proving God's love; those reconciled through His death will be saved through His life.
Sin and death enter through one man, and death reigns even before the law.
Adam's trespass brings condemnation, while Jesus's obedience brings justification, righteousness, and life.
Where the law increases trespass, God's grace overflows still more and brings eternal life through Jesus.

title: Freed from Sin to Serve God
summary_text: Paul rejects the idea that people should keep sinning so God's grace can increase. Through baptism, believers share Christ's death and burial and walk in new life, freed from sin's slavery. Paul calls them to live for God and offer their bodies for righteousness rather than evil. Grace does not excuse sin: people serve the master they obey, and serving God leads to holiness. Sin pays death as its wage, but God gives eternal life through Jesus as a gift.
key_points: Paul rejects continued sin and connects baptism with sharing Jesus's death, burial, and new life.
Believers' old self was crucified with Christ to break slavery to sin, and they will share His resurrection.
Paul calls believers to offer their bodies to God rather than let sin rule them.
Living under grace does not excuse sin; people become slaves of the master they obey.
Sin ends in death, while serving God leads to holiness and His gift of eternal life.

title: God's Holy Law Exposes Sin's Power
summary_text: Using marriage as an example, Paul explains that death releases a person from the law's authority. Believers have died to the law through Jesus so they can belong to the risen Christ and serve through the Spirit. Paul insists that the law is holy, while sin uses its commandment against coveting to stir wrong desires, deceive, and bring death. He then speaks of wanting to obey God's law but doing the evil he hates, with sin holding him captive. His cry for rescue leads to thanks to God through Jesus, though he ends by describing his mind serving God's law and his flesh serving sin's law.
key_points: Paul uses a marriage ending at death to explain release from the law through Jesus.
Release from the law allows believers to serve through the Spirit rather than the written code.
The law is holy, righteous, and good, but sin exploits its commandment to produce coveting, deception, and death.
Paul describes wanting what is good while sin produces the opposite actions and holds him captive.
A cry for rescue leads to thanks through Jesus and a final contrast between service in the mind and in the flesh.

title: Life in the Spirit and Unbreakable Love
summary_text: Those in Christ Jesus face no condemnation: God condemned sin in the flesh through His Son, and His Spirit gives life. The Spirit leads God's children, who wait with creation through suffering in hope of future glory. The Spirit intercedes as they pray, and God works for the good of those who love Him and are called for His purpose. Those God foreknew He also predestined to become like His Son, then called, justified, and glorified. Paul ends sure that no suffering, power, or created thing can separate them from God's love in Jesus, who intercedes for them.
key_points: God condemns sin through His Son; the Spirit's law brings freedom and life, unlike the flesh's hostility toward God.
The Spirit confirms believers' adoption as sons of God and heirs, sharing glory with Christ if they share His suffering.
Creation and believers groan in suffering, saved in hope while awaiting freedom, glory, and the redemption of their bodies.
The Spirit intercedes for believers, and God foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified those He brings into His Son's likeness.
God justifies His elect, Christ intercedes for them, and nothing in creation can cut them off from God's love in Him.

title: God's Promise, His Election, and Israel's Stumbling
summary_text: Paul grieves for Israel, whose gifts include divine glory and the family line of Christ, whom he calls God over all. God's word has not failed: Isaac and Rebecca's twins show that His election rests on His call, not their works. God raised Pharaoh to show His power and shows mercy or hardens as He chooses; Paul answers a question about blame with a potter's right to shape clay. Prophets speak of God calling Gentiles His people and saving a remnant of Israel. Paul ends with Gentiles receiving righteousness by faith, while Israel fails in its quest through works and stumbles over God's stone in Zion.
key_points: Paul mourns for Israel, lists its gifts, and calls Christ, born from its people, God over all.
Isaac and Rebecca's twins illustrate God's promise and election rather than mere ancestry or works.
Paul rejects the charge of injustice and uses Pharaoh to discuss God's freedom to show mercy or harden.
Paul uses a potter's authority to answer blame, discusses vessels of wrath and mercy, and cites prophets about Gentiles and Israel's remnant.
Gentiles receive righteousness by faith, while Israel pursues it through works and stumbles over God's stone.

title: Salvation Through Faith and Hearing Christ's Word
summary_text: Paul prays that Israel will be saved, but says its people seek their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's. He calls Christ the end of the law, bringing righteousness to believers, and says the word of faith is near. People are justified by believing that God raised Jesus and are saved as they confess Him as Lord, with the same promise for Jews and Greeks. Calling on the Lord requires faith, which comes through hearing Christ's word from those sent to preach the gospel. Paul says Israel has heard, and ends with God revealing Himself to those who did not seek Him and reaching out to a stubborn people.
key_points: Paul longs for Israel's salvation but says its zeal misses God's righteousness, which comes through Christ for believers.
The word of faith is near: belief in Jesus's resurrection and confession of Him as Lord bring justification and salvation.
The same Lord welcomes Jews and Greeks, saving all who call on Him.
Calling requires belief, belief requires hearing, and hearing requires messengers sent to proclaim Christ's word.
Israel has heard, and Scripture depicts God revealing Himself to unexpected people while reaching toward those who resist Him.

title: Israel, the Gentiles, and God's Mercy
summary_text: God has not cast off His people: Paul points to a remnant chosen by grace, not works, while others are hardened. Israel's trespass has brought salvation to the Gentiles, and Paul hopes this will stir his own people to return. Using an olive tree, he warns Gentiles not to boast, since they stand by faith and God can cut them off or restore broken branches. He says Israel's hardening is in part until the Gentiles' full number comes in, and all Israel will be saved through God's covenant to remove sins. God's gifts and call stand, and Paul ends in praise of His mercy and wisdom.
key_points: God has not rejected those He foreknew; a remnant chosen by grace remains, while others are hardened.
As apostle to the Gentiles, Paul hopes their salvation will stir Israel, whose rejection has meant reconciliation for the world.
Gentiles grafted into the olive tree must fear rather than boast, since God can cut them off and restore unbelieving branches.
Paul announces Israel's partial hardening and salvation, affirming God's covenant and lasting election for the patriarchs' sake despite opposition to the gospel.
God consigns all to disobedience to show mercy to all, and Paul praises His wisdom and glory.

title: Living Sacrifices and Sincere Love
summary_text: Because of God's mercy, Paul calls believers to offer themselves as holy, living sacrifices and let their minds be renewed to recognize His will. They must think humbly about themselves and use their different gifts of grace as members of one body in Christ. Paul describes sincere love through mutual honor, service, hope, prayer, and care for saints in need. He tells them to bless persecutors, share others' joys and griefs, and seek peace without pride. Instead of taking revenge, they must leave room for God's wrath and answer an enemy's needs with good.
key_points: Paul urges worship through living sacrifices and renewed minds that can recognize God's will.
Believers must think humbly and use gifts such as prophecy and service according to grace and faith.
Sincere love includes honoring others, serving the Lord, patient hope, prayer, and sharing with needy saints.
Believers must bless rather than curse persecutors, share others' feelings, and avoid pride.
Paul forbids revenge, urges peace wherever possible, and commands care for enemies instead of repayment of evil.

title: Honor Authority, Love Neighbors, and Wake Up
summary_text: Paul tells believers to submit to rulers, whose power comes from God and whose task is to punish wrong. They must pay what they owe in taxes, respect, and honor, and obey for the sake of conscience too. Love remains a debt, since love does no harm to a neighbor and thus fulfills the law's commands. With salvation nearer, Paul calls them to wake up, leave deeds of darkness, and put on light as armor. They must live decently, clothe themselves with the Lord Jesus Christ, and stop feeding the flesh's desires.
key_points: Paul says resisting governing authority opposes God's appointment and brings judgment, while submission is also a matter of conscience.
Taxes and other dues must be paid, along with the respect and honor owed to others.
Love fulfills the law because it harms no neighbor and sums up the commandments.
Nearer salvation calls for wakefulness, decent conduct, and putting on Christ rather than feeding the flesh's desires.

title: Welcome One Another Without Causing Stumbling
summary_text: Paul tells believers to welcome those whose faith is weak without quarreling over food and days. Those who eat and those who abstain can both honor the Lord, and all belong to Christ in life and death and must answer to God. Paul considers food clean in itself, but urges believers not to harm someone who regards it as unclean. The kingdom of God concerns righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, so love must guide eating and drinking. Anyone who eats while doubting is condemned, because acting apart from faith is sin.
key_points: Believers must not despise or judge each other over food and observed days, since each serves the Lord.
Christ died and lived again as Lord of living and dead, and each person will face God's judgment.
Paul says nothing is unclean in itself, yet love forbids using food in a way that harms another believer.
God's kingdom centers on righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, so believers must build each other up.
A person who eats against his doubts is condemned because the act does not come from faith.

title: Welcome One Another as Paul's Mission Continues
summary_text: Paul calls the strong to bear with the weak and welcome each other as Christ has welcomed them, with hope drawn from Scripture. Christ serves the circumcised to confirm God's promises, while Gentiles glorify God for His mercy. Paul serves the gospel so that Gentiles may be an offering sanctified by the Holy Spirit, and seeks to preach where Christ is not known. He plans to take aid to poor saints in Jerusalem, then visit the believers on his way to Spain. He asks for prayer for safety, a welcome for his service, and a joyful visit.
key_points: Christ's example and Scripture's encouragement call believers to bear with the weak and praise God together.
Christ confirms promises to the patriarchs, and Scripture speaks of Gentiles praising God and hoping in Him.
By God's grace, Paul serves the gospel so that Gentiles may become an offering sanctified by the Holy Spirit.
Paul plans to bring aid to Jerusalem's poor saints, then visit the believers on his way to Spain.
Paul requests prayer for protection in Judea, a welcome for his Jerusalem service, and a refreshing visit with the believers.

title: Greetings, a Warning, and Praise to God
summary_text: Paul asks the believers to welcome Phoebe and help her, since she has helped him and many others. He greets workers and saints, including Prisca and Aquila, who risked their lives for him in their service to Christ. He warns against teachers who divide and deceive, and says the God of peace will soon crush Satan beneath their feet. Friends with Paul send greetings, including Tertius, who wrote the letter down. Paul gives glory to the wise God, who makes believers strong through the gospel and has made His mystery known to bring nations to faith and obedience.
key_points: Paul commends Phoebe's service and help and asks that she receive a welcome and any assistance she needs.
Paul greets Prisca and Aquila and others, including Andronicus and Junia, whom he describes as outstanding among the apostles.
The believers must avoid divisive deceivers, remain wise in good, and expect God to crush Satan beneath their feet.
Timothy, Tertius, Gaius, and other companions send greetings to the believers.
Paul praises God for the revealed gospel mystery, made known through the prophets' writings to bring nations to obedient faith.
